query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the spray stand‐off distance by 20–30% will enhance particle kinetic energy, thereby increasing deposition efficiency and coating thickness while preserving minimal oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high‐entropy alloy powder with a 15–45 μm feedstock deposited using a conventional stand‐off distance that currently yields sub-optimal thickness.
generation.intervention: Decrease the stand‐off distance by approximately 20–30% (e.g., from around 250 mm to 175–200 mm) without altering any other process parameters.
generation.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition (via HVOF or APS) performed under a controlled atmosphere with a constant powder feeding rate and substrate preparation typical of bond coat applications in thermal barrier coating systems.
generation.structural_mediator: A shorter stand‐off distance decreases the flight time of particles, increasing their kinetic energy upon impact and reducing in-flight oxidation.
generation.mechanism: A reduced stand‐off distance minimizes particle scattering and oxygen exposure time during flight, thus enhancing particle momentum for better splat flattening and bonding. This increases coating thickness while keeping oxidation similar or reduced relative to the baseline.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coating thickness increases by at least 30% relative to the baseline while as-sprayed oxidation levels remain similar or lower, confirmed by oxide analysis and splat morphology studies.
generation.baseline: Coatings produced at the standard stand‐off distance (e.g., 250 mm) using 15–45 μm feedstock with known sub-optimal thickness and minimal oxidation.
generation.boundary: The stand‐off distance must not be reduced to the point of causing substrate overheating or excessive particle rebound; the optimal range is defined where kinetic energy gains are balanced with proper particle temperature control.
generation.uncertainty: There is sensitivity to small changes in distance; any non-uniformity in particle size distribution might interact with the effect of decreased stand-off, necessitating careful process monitoring.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of deposition runs at stand‐off distances of 250 mm (baseline), 225 mm, 200 mm, and 175 mm while keeping all other parameters constant. Analyze the resulting coating for thickness and oxidation state via cross-sectional imaging and chemical analysis.
measurements: Coating thickness via cross-sectional SEM or optical microscopy
Oxide content via XPS or EDS analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If reducing the stand‐off distance does not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness, or if oxidation levels are significantly higher than the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 4 shows the difference in the properties based on the spraying distance. As the spraying distance increases, the average thickness of the coatings slightly decreases due to a stronger scattering of the particles on the longer path. An increase in the spraying distance results in an increase in coating porosity. Porosity depends on the temperature and kinetic energy of the particles []. Particles sprayed from a longer distance have a lower kinetic energy when they strike the substrate, which results in increased porosity. High temperatures and exposure to oxygen lead to the in-flight oxidation of particles; the smaller particles undergo more severe oxidation. With an increase in the spraying distance, the particles are exposed to oxygen for a longer time, which leads to an increased content of oxides (Figure 4d). As the particles oxidize with the formation of alumina, BCC solid solution loses aluminum, which is reflected in a decrease in its lattice parameter (Figure 3b). papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder.
papers.system: FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy (closely related to FeCoNiCrAl systems)
papers.approach: Gas-atomized powder deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel (HVOF) spraying; experiments varied the nozzle-to-substrate spraying distance
papers.findings: An increase in the spraying distance led to slightly decreased coating thickness due to stronger particle scattering and increased porosity; longer flight times increased in‐flight oxidation, altering phase composition (e.g. depletion of Al in the BCC phase triggering transformation to FCC near the surface).
papers.mechanism: Shorter flight distances improve particle kinetic energy on impact, reducing oxygen exposure time and limiting in-flight oxidation, whereas longer distances allow more oxidation and scattering that thin the deposit.

papers.title: Microstructure and Corrosion Behavior of Atmospheric Plasma Sprayed NiCoCrAlFe High Entropy Alloy Coating.
papers.system: NiCoCrAlFe high-entropy alloy coating (analogous in composition and performance requirements to FeCoNiCrAl systems)
papers.approach: Atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) deposition, with post-deposition annealing used to promote phase formation and assess coating integrity
papers.findings: APS coatings displayed multi-phase lamellar structures with evidence of in-flight oxidation (presence of spinel oxides). Process parameters (stand-off distance, plasma energy) strongly affected coating porosity, splat formation, and ultimately, the integrity and corrosion resistance of the deposit.
papers.mechanism: Control of the thermal and kinetic energy during spraying influences splat flattening, particle oxidation and subsequent microstructure, leading to trade-offs between coating thickness, oxidation levels, and mechanical integrity.

papers.title: Microstructural Evolution of AlCoCrFeNiSi High-Entropy Alloy Powder during Mechanical Alloying and Its Coating Performance.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy, a ductility–brittleness system sharing similarities with FeCoNiCrAl alloys
papers.approach: Mechanical alloying to optimize powder morphology and particle size distribution, followed by atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) deposition
papers.findings: Feedstock particle shape and size distribution strongly impact spray dynamics: near-equiaxed and appropriately sized particles provided better flowability and splat formation, resulting in coherent, dense coatings with relatively uniform microstructure.
papers.mechanism: Optimized particle morphology enhances in-flight melting and flattening upon impact, leading to uniform splat formation while controlling oxidation by reducing the exposed surface area during flight.

established: Shorter spray distances yield coatings with higher deposition efficiency and thickness due to higher particle kinetic energy and reduced flight time, minimizing oxidation.
Thermal-spray processes (HVOF and APS) inherently expose particles to high temperatures and oxygen, leading to in-flight oxidation that affects phase constitution and coating microstructure.
Feedstock particle size and morphology are critical; near-equiaxed, appropriately sized particles enhance flowability and deposition quality.

approaches_tried.outcome: Shorter distances improved kinetic energy and deposition yielding thicker coatings, while longer distances increased oxidation and porosity.

approaches_tried.approach: Optimizing powder morphology via mechanical alloying
approaches_tried.outcome: Produced feedstock with improved flowability and enhanced splat formation leading to denser APS coatings with controlled oxidation.

approaches_tried.approach: Post-spray annealing to form more uniform phases
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced coating properties such as microhardness and corrosion resistance, though not directly addressing coating thickness.

mechanisms: Higher particle kinetic energy (from reduced spray distance or increased feed rate) increases deposition efficiency and splat flattening while reducing oxidation exposure time.
In-flight oxidation alters feedstock composition by depleting reactive elements (e.g., Al), thereby modifying the phase stability of the deposited coating.
Powder morphology affects melting behavior and splat formation, influencing the ultimate coating density and integrity.
disagreements: Some studies indicate that in-flight oxidation (forming oxides like alumina or spinels) can enhance hardness and wear resistance, whereas for bond coat applications minimal oxidation is desired to maintain interface integrity.

There is variability in the reported trade-offs between operation parameters (e.g., spray distance, heating rate) versus coating thickness and oxidation, leading to different interpretations of the optimal balance.
open_questions: Can a single process parameter adjustment—such as a reduced stand-off distance—consistently overcome thickness shortfalls while keeping as-sprayed oxidation minimal in FeCoNiCrAl coatings?
How does the interplay between feedstock particle size distribution and spray distance specifically affect the deposition yield and oxidation kinetics for FeCoNiCrAl systems?
What is the quantitative relationship between particle momentum (kinetic energy) and the resulting coating thickness and oxidation level in high-entropy alloy bond coats?
opportunities: Investigate the effect of reducing the spray stand-off distance as a single intervention, thereby increasing particle kinetic energy, potentially overcoming the thickness shortfall while limiting oxidation.

Combine controlled feedstock optimization (e.g., using a tailored particle size range from 15–45 μm) with a reduced spray distance to maximize deposition efficiency without compromising coating integrity.

Conduct controlled experiments varying only the spray distance (or an equivalent parameter affecting particle momentum) under service conditions relevant to thermal barrier coating systems to establish clear falsification criteria based on coating thickness and oxidation measurements.

directions.assessment: Directly increases particle kinetic energy and reduces in‐flight oxidation by shortening residence time. Supported by evidence showing that shorter distances yield thicker, denser coatings (e.g. PMC10820071::web::010::3_2_oxidation_and_phase_transformations_). Highly feasible and effective for thermal-spray deposition if boundary conditions (avoiding substrate overheating) are respected.

Can improve deposition efficiency by supplying more material per unit time. Evidence in spray parameter studies supports that higher feed rates lower dilution (e.g. PMC11857518::web::013::3_2_dilution_rate_mathematical_model_and). However, care is needed to avoid excessive particle overlap or altered splat formation.

directions.direction: Increase the energy input (e.g. fuel flow/combustion power) to boost particle velocity
directions.assessment: Enhancing the combustion energy increases particle momentum, improving splat flattening and deposition yield. Literature suggests that higher particle speeds can contribute to thicker deposits; however, elevated temperatures can risk oxidation if not controlled.

directions.direction: Enhance inert gas shielding by adjusting carrier gas composition/flow
directions.assessment: Increasing the fraction or flow of an inert gas (e.g. argon) minimizes oxygen exposure, which can permit a reduced stand‐off distance without increasing oxidation. This intervention builds on inert atmosphere techniques and is supported indirectly by coating studies that note the importance of oxygen control (e.g. PMC8875499::web::007::2_3_atmospheric_plasma_spraying_coating_).

directions.direction: Moderate substrate preheating to optimize splat adhesion
directions.assessment: Elevating substrate temperature modestly can improve particle bonding and deposition efficiency, potentially increasing thickness. However, the risk is that excessive preheating might exacerbate oxidation; the physics is sound but it is a more indirect influence on thickness.
